newsitem.title: USA: Murkowski clears Pena's nomination for vote.
newsitem.headline: Murkowski clears Pena's nomination for vote.

text.p: Senate Energy Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski Tuesday agreed to let his committee vote on the nomination of Federico Pena as energy secretary, saying he had captured the White House's attention on the issue of nuclear waste storage.
The Energy Committee is slated to vote Thursday on Pena, and the full Senate should vote on the nomination within the next couple of weeks, Murkowski said at a news conference.

The Alaska Republican said he agreed to allow Pena's confirmation because the White House indicated it was willing to work with his committee on the issue of building a central dump site for radioactive waste accumulating at nuclear power plants across the country.

"I delayed the vote in large part because the administration has refused to confront an important environmental issue," Murkowski said. "Now they seem willing to face the issue. And they are beginning to sort out their real position."
Murkowski also said he will push legislation to build an interim nuclear waste dump in Nevada, even though the administration indicated Clinton would veto it.

A letter from White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles said Clinton still would veto any legislation that designated an interim storage site before a study was completed on using Nevada's Yucca Mountain as a permanent dump.
Clinton's veto threat killed the bill last year, but Murkowski said he was willing to make changes and see how the administration would respond this year.

The White House has said Murkowski's bill would divert resources from the long-term storage facility and would prejudge Nevada as the permanent nuclear dump site. The Yucca study is to be ready next year.

The federal government in January legally becomes responsible for tons of waste from power reactors scattered at some 80 sites across the country, but it will not have a permanent respository ready before 2010 or 2015.
Environmental groups opposed to Murkowski's plan to ship radioactive waste to Nevada said they were pleased that the White House stood up to the committee chairman.

"Murkowski and Bowles met eye-to-eye and Murkowski blinked. The administration has not backed off one inch and Murkowski is trying to spin it his way to save face," Bill Magavern, director of Public Citizen's Critical Mass Energy Project, said.

Asked if the administration had changed its position on interim storage, an Energy Department spokeswoman said Bowles' letter "was consistent with Secretary Pena's testimony before the Senate Energy Committee" in January.

Nuclear power utilities that have paid some $12 billion into a fund for the federal government to store their waste support Murkowski's bill, while some environmentalists hope the build-up of wastes onsite will force reactors to close.
Murkowski said the federal government faces up to $80 billion in liabilities from the accumulating waste.
